claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys with larger lattice distortions have superior structural stability at high temperatures.
High-entropy nanoalloys with larger lattice distortions have superior chemical stability at high temperatures.
Diversity in constituent atomic sizes produces severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion induces sluggish atomic diffusion.
Sluggish atomic diffusion delays grain growth.
Sluggish atomic diffusion delays phase separation and precipitation.
Sluggish atomic diffusion suppresses rapid chemical segregation.
Sluggish atomic diffusion delays deleterious oxidation and oxide growth.
Refractory equiatomic high-entropy alloys can be fabricated by laser-based additive manufacturing from elemental powder mixtures.
Small compositional modifications can vary atomic-size mismatch while preserving a similar overall phase structure.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch increases lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion lowers high-temperature diffusion coefficients.
Lower diffusion coefficients impede rearrangement into deleterious clusters or precipitates.
Impeded transport of oxidizable species slows oxidation.
Relative to a lower-distortion baseline, a higher-distortion alloy will exhibit reduced grain growth, less phase separation or precipitation, and slower oxidation kinetics.
The prediction applies at approximately 800–1100 °C while the nanoalloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
If the alloy becomes multiphase, precipitation-related or other microstructural mechanisms may dominate its high-temperature behavior.
Dynamic recrystallization can become important under elevated-temperature deformation conditions.
The relative importance of protective-oxide formation and diffusion-controlled oxidation varies with alloy system and environment.
